title: These AI-Powered Pool Robots Are on Sale—and They Basically Do Everything
summary: Summer is coming, and with it, the eternal struggle: keeping the pool clean. But what if you could outsource the gross stuff to a robot that's smarter than your average vacuum? Beatbot's lineup of pool-cleaning robots is on sale through the end of May, and they're some of the most advanced on the market. The star of the show is the Beatbot Sora 50, a top-shelf machine that does it all. It skims the surface, scrubs floors, walls, and the waterline with five brushes, and even uses AI to detect debris—meaning it can tell the difference between a leaf and a shadow, and zero in on the dirt. It runs for up to six hours, then autonomously returns to the surface and floats when the job is done or the battery is low. At 29 pounds, it's a bit hefty to lift out, but the trade-off is never manually cleaning your pool again. For those who don't need surface skimming, the mid-range Sora 30 handles walls, waterline, shallow areas, and floors for five hours. It also returns on its own, and you can retrieve it with a single tap in the app, which lets you set schedules, monitor temperature, and adjust speed. The entry-level skimmer is slow and methodical—it won't slam into walls—and features a 9-liter basket with solar and magnetic wireless charging. All models connect to an app, giving you control like a video game. Whether you're tired of paying the pool guy or just don't want to deal with whatever scary stuff is floating in the water, these robots offer a hassle-free solution. Just in time for cannonball season.
why_it_matters: AI-driven home robots like these pool cleaners represent a shift toward automation in daily life, potentially reducing manual labor but also raising conversations about electronic waste and the growing reliance on technology for simple tasks.

background_read: Beatbot, a newer entrant in the home robotics market, is part of a wave of companies using artificial intelligence to make domestic chores fully automatic.
Robotic pool cleaners date back to the 1980s, when devices like the Aquabot first arrived, but early models moved randomly and could not distinguish dirt from shadows.
Wireless charging technology, which uses magnetic induction to power devices without cables, is increasingly appearing in outdoor appliances to reduce electrical hazards near water.
The pool industry often sees a spike in sales during May, as homeowners in the Northern Hemisphere prepare for the summer swimming season.
Solar-powered pool devices tap into renewable energy, aligning with broader environmental efforts to reduce carbon footprints.

perspectives.description: These robots eliminate a tedious chore, letting pool owners spend more time enjoying the water. The AI's ability to distinguish debris from shadows means cleaner pools with less waste of energy and chemicals, and the app integration offers convenient, game-like control.

High upfront costs and the 29-pound weight of the model make it less accessible for smaller homes or those with physical limitations. Moreover, reliance on proprietary batteries and software could mean expensive repairs or early obsolescence, adding to the growing e-waste problem.

The adoption of AI and wireless charging in pool cleaners mirrors larger trends in consumer electronics, where devices become more autonomous but also more complex. This shift may increase efficiency, but it also concentrates technical expertise in the hands of manufacturers, reducing user repairability.

Future iterations might incorporate water quality sensors and automatic chemical dosing, turning these robots into full-fledged pool maintenance systems. However, this could also lead to subscription models and data collection on usage patterns, raising privacy concerns.
